title: The Sphinx and the hunt for lost magic
summary: Why mages began seeking surviving old ways around 2000.

claims.text: With the Avatar Storm raging, Masters missing and the Technocracy entrenched, the Traditions look to old arts that still have living keepers somewhere.
Those keepers are few and often hide, either despising the modern world or guarding powers that rivals want buried.
The Rogue Council, signing as the Sphinx, sends clues urging mages to seek these survivors; the Technocracy receives messages too, and some fear the aim is open war between the two sides.

title: Moko
summary: Maori facial markings among Awakened and Sleepers.

claims.text: Maori moko record a wearer's rank, trade, family line and skill; a tohunga, the Maori word for a mage, bears marks that show whether the bearer is Initiate, Adept or Master.
Moko are cut with a fine chisel of greenstone or albatross bone, leaving grooves in the skin as well as color.
Seidr workers use a brewing cauldron for poisons, potions, herbal work and sympathetic magic, the cauldron standing for the churning wyrd they seek to steer.
Rune workers usually carve their own set of the 24 Elder Futhark runes in ash, stone or antler, or use an inherited set; casting a few for divination is the most basic use.

title: The Picts in mage lore
summary: What scholars of the Awakened say of the northern Britons.

claims.text: Little is known of the Picts beyond Roman reports and Celtic tales of northern clans hostile to Rome, and their origin is disputed.
Their royal line passed through the mother: a king's sister bore the next heir, a custom some tie to a bargain for Irish brides.

title: The Etruscans
summary: The old masters of central Italy.

claims.text: The Etruscans are said to have come from Lydia after the Trojan War and founded a league of 12 city-states, among them Tarchna and Veii.
For over a millennium they led Italy, and Romans later called Etruria the source of every superstition; their own founding of Rome brought about their fall.
In Roman arenas a figure dressed as Charun came out with a hammer to end the dying, and an echo survives in the rite of tapping a dead Pope's brow with a small silver hammer.
Some ask whether Charun was truly a demon of death or a mage who made the hammer and was later remembered as the death-god because the hammer worked so well.
The hammer is steeped in Entropy and grants authority over the Charontes, the spirits that serve it.
